issues.legal_issue: A statute permitting a municipality to impose specified taxes in only part of its area is not discriminatory when the statute provides clear guidance connecting taxation with the provision of municipal duties and amenities.
material_facts: The statute authorized taxes to be imposed throughout a municipality or in any part of it and assigned municipalities obligatory duties and discretionary functions, including the provision of special amenities.

The court found that municipal duties and amenities could be provided in different parts of a municipality at different times or in response to differing local needs, and that taxation in a part could fund the special treatment of that part.
issues.conclusion: The statutory power to impose taxes in part of a municipality did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality because the statute, read as a whole, supplied legislative guidance for exercising that power.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, a law leaving selection or classification to an authority is valid if the statute itself expressly or by necessary implication supplies a clear policy or guidance. The court applied Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, Dwarka Prasad Laxmi Narain v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Dhirendra Krishna Mondol v. Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra, P. Balakotaiah v. Union of India, and M/s. Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India. It read sections 7, 8 and 128 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act together: municipal duties and amenities could require separate treatment of different areas, while the tax power could fund that treatment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_municipal_ta: A person challenges the constitutionality of a municipality’s authority to impose taxes in a selected area.
predicates.statute_authorizes_taxation_in_a_part_of: The governing law permits municipal taxes to be imposed in less than the whole municipal area.
predicates.statute_links_municipal_revenue_to_dutie: The governing law connects municipal taxation with carrying out municipal duties or providing amenities.
predicates.municipal_needs_can_differ_by_area: The municipality’s duties or amenity needs may require different treatment in different areas or at different times.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns authority to tax only part of a municipality, the rule permits that authority where the law links tax revenue to municipal duties or amenities and local needs can differ by area.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal tax confined to a geographically distinct area does not violate equality when the area’s special amenities and the expense of serving it reasonably relate to the geographical classification.
material_facts: The municipality developed the area as a separate unit and provided it with broad roads, larger plots, parks and gardens, special lighting, footpaths, water booths and special sanitary arrangements.
The older area consisted of congested localities, small houses and narrow lanes.

The municipality collected nightsoil and rubbish from each bungalow in the separately treated area, while in the older area collection took place from a common point in each ward, making the former method more expensive.
House and scavenging taxes were imposed in the separately developed area.
issues.conclusion: The geographical classification had a reasonable relation to the taxes imposed and did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits geographical classification where the difference between geographical units reasonably relates to the object of the law. In applying the classification doctrine to taxation, courts allow the legislature a wide range and flexibility, while retaining the requirement of a reasonable relation. The court relied on Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer, Kasaragod, Purshottam Govindji v. B. M. Desai, K. T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, and Bareilly Municipality v. Kundan Lal.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_geographical: A person challenges the equality of a municipal tax imposed only in a selected geographical area.
predicates.tax_applies_only_to_a_distinct_area: The municipality imposes the tax in one area rather than uniformly throughout the municipality.
predicates.distinct_area_receives_special_amenities: The selected area receives special amenities or municipal services that cost more to provide there.
predicates.area_difference_is_reasonably_related_to: The differences between the selected area and other areas reasonably relate to imposing the tax in the selected area.

issues.definition: A geographically limited municipal tax is not discriminatory where it applies to a distinct area that receives special amenities or costlier services and those differences reasonably relate to the tax.

issues.legal_issue: A municipality’s power to set tax rates and identify liable persons or classes is not arbitrary when the tax is confined to authorized taxable subjects and the setting of rates and liability is subject to an opportunity to object and governmental review.
material_facts: The law separately identified the subjects on which a municipality could levy taxes.
The municipality had to make and publish proposals specifying the tax, the rate and the persons or classes liable.
Inhabitants could submit objections, which the municipality had to consider; the proposals and objections were then subject to review by the prescribed authority and the State Government.
issues.conclusion: The statutory scheme did not confer arbitrary power on the municipality in violation of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a municipal tax-setting process where the taxing authority is confined to specified taxable subjects and rates and liability are determined through a procedure allowing affected persons to object and providing governmental review. The court read sections 128 and 131–133 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act together.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_municipal_ta: A person challenges the constitutionality of the municipality’s power to determine tax rates or liable persons.
predicates.law_limits_taxation_to_specified_subject: The governing law confines municipal taxes to specified taxable subjects.
predicates.affected_people_can_object_to_rates_or_l: The procedure allows affected people to object to proposed rates or to the persons made liable.
predicates.proposals_receive_governmental_review: The proposed tax arrangements are subject to review by a governmental authority.

issues.definition: A municipal tax-setting power is not arbitrary where the law limits taxable subjects, affected people may object to rates or liability, and the proposals receive governmental review.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge alleging that a municipal tax was imposed contrary to statutory procedure fails when the alleged procedural violation is not established by the record.
material_facts: The petitioner alleged that the municipal proposals did not contain all required details, and the municipality denied that allegation.
A municipal resolution referred to draft proposals for revising the tax, but those drafts were not before the court.
The petitioner did not specifically allege that the government had failed to make rules in accordance with the statutory procedure.
The taxes had been imposed long before the challenge, but the court treated the passage of time as insufficient to excuse an established departure from statutory requirements.
issues.conclusion: It was not established that the taxes had been imposed in violation of the statutory procedure, so the challenge based on infringement of the right under Article 19(1)(f) failed.
issues.legal_principle: No tax may be levied or collected except in accordance with law, and an established departure from statutory requirements may infringe Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. A statutory authority’s order is presumed to have followed the prescribed procedure, but long acquiescence cannot cure an established illegality. The court considered sections 131–136 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act and found no established procedural breach.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_tax_procedure: A taxpayer challenges a municipal tax on the ground that the statutory procedure for imposing it was not followed.
predicates.municipal_record_refers_to_required_prop: The municipal record contains a resolution referring to draft proposals for the tax.
predicates.no_evidence_establishes_procedural_failu: The record does not establish that the municipality omitted a required procedural step.
predicates.no_specific_allegation_identifies_anothe: The taxpayer does not specifically allege a separate procedural defect for which the record supplies no proof.

issues.definition: A procedural challenge to a municipal tax does not establish illegality where the municipal record refers to the required proposals and no evidence or specific allegation establishes a procedural failure.

issues.legal_issue: A mistaken reference in a tax notification to a statutory clause does not invalidate the tax when the municipality had power to impose the tax on the subject described in the notification.
material_facts: The notification described a tax for removing nightsoil and rubbish from buildings in the selected area but referred to the clause concerning cleaning latrines and privies.
The municipality stated that the clause reference was a mistake and that the broader scavenging-tax clause was intended.
The municipality collected nightsoil and rubbish from each bungalow, a combined service that the court held fell within its power to impose a scavenging tax.
issues.conclusion: The municipality had power to impose the scavenging tax, and the mistaken reference to another clause in the notification did not affect that power or invalidate the tax.
issues.legal_principle: The validity of a tax depends on whether the taxing authority has power to tax the subject; a mistaken statutory reference does not defeat an existing power to impose the tax. The court distinguished the scavenging-tax power in section 128(1)(xi) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act from the power in section 128(1)(xii) to tax the cleaning of latrines and privies, and held the described combined service within the former power.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_tax_notification: A taxpayer challenges a municipal tax because the notification imposing it refers to a statutory clause.
predicates.notification_describes_a_taxable_municip: The notification describes a municipal service that is the subject of the tax.
predicates.municipality_has_power_to_tax_that_servi: The municipality has statutory authority to impose a tax on the service described.
predicates.notification_cites_the_wrong_taxing_clau: The notification cites a clause other than the one that supplies the municipality’s authority to impose the tax.

issues.definition: A mistaken clause reference does not invalidate a municipal tax where the notification describes a taxable service and the municipality has authority to tax that service.
